messages.subject: Meta-mixture models?
parts:
Hey everyone,

I have a fairly high dimensional model in JAGS that I want to implement in Stan due to high autocorrelation.

I created a toy-model in Stan that has similar concepts to the model I will ultimately run.

In essence, it is a mixture of mixture models.
I want the p(k=2|D), or the probability of a k=2 mixture model.

Within the k=1 model (non-mixture), y is normally distributed around some N of unknown mu and sd.
Within the k=2 model, individuals have some probability of belonging to model 1 or model 2, where 1 and 2 are both normals with unknown parameters, and mu_2 > mu_1.
Individual probabilities are distributed as Dirichlet with unknown parameters, whose parameters are in turn dirichlet(1,...,1). (I'm using dirichlet instead of beta because the model should extend to more than just k=1 or k=2).

The likelihood is thus weighted by p(k=1|D) and p(k=2|D), and within the k=2, weighted by p(k_i=1|D) and p(k_i=2|D).

The problem is that the chains come to different solutions, and the parameter of interest, pk[2], is very poorly mixing.
What could I do to improve convergence?

Here is the full model:

x1 <- rnorm(100)
x2 <- rnorm(50,5,2)
x <- c(x1,x2)

mixMeta <- "
data {
    int N;
    vector[N] y;
}
transformed data {
    int Kappa;
    Kappa <- 2;
}

parameters {
    simplex[Kappa] pk; //p(K = 1), p(K=2)
    // Problem: We need several simplex arrays for each K model; can't use simplex theta[N], because all simplexes must be specified
    // For the time being, I'm doing this manually, assuming Kappa = 2
    simplex[2] theta_2[N]; //p(k_i = 1) in K=2
    simplex[2] alpha_2; //p(k = 1) in K = 2

    vector[1] mu_1; //mu in K = 1
    vector[2] mu_2s; //unsorted mu, to be sorted later

    vector<lower=0>[1] sigma_1;
    vector<lower=0>[2] sigma_2;
}
transformed parameters{
    ordered[2] mu_2;
    mu_2 <- sort_asc(mu_2s);
}
model {
    vector[2] lp;
    vector[2] lp_s;
// Priors
    // Means
    mu_1 ~ normal(0,5);
    mu_2 ~ normal(0,5);

    // SDs
    sigma_1 ~ cauchy(0,5);
    sigma_2 ~ cauchy(0,5);

    // theta weights (within K models)
    for(i in 1:N){
        theta_2[i] ~ dirichlet(alpha_2);
    }
    alpha_2 ~ dirichlet(rep_vector(1.0,2));

// Likelihoods
    for(i in 1:N){
        // K = 1
        lp[1] <- log(pk[1]) + normal_log(y[i],mu_1,sigma_1);

        // K = 2
        lp_s[1] <- log(theta_2[i,1]) + normal_log(y[i],mu_2[1],sigma_2[1]);
        lp_s[2] <- log(theta_2[i,2]) + normal_log(y[i],mu_2[2],sigma_2[2]);
        lp[2] <- log(pk[2]) + log_sum_exp(lp_s[1],lp_s[2]);

        // Increment
        increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(lp));
    }
}
"

# Label switching problem; cycles between labels
# One solution is to use an ordered vector (ordered) and use softmax to produce an ordered simplex
# Another is to constrain mu_2 to be > mu_1 through a constraint
stanOut <- stan(model_code = mixMeta,data = list(y=x,N=150),chains = 4,cores=4,iter = 10000,thin=4)

parts:
This doesn't help with mixing, but it's more efficient
computationally to use a single prior with a beta
prior than a simplex[2] with a Dirichlet prior (the
second component of the simplex is just one minus the
first).

And rather than this:

> vector[2] mu_2s; //unsorted mu, to be sorted later
>
> vector<lower=0>[1] sigma_1;
> vector<lower=0>[2] sigma_2;
> }
> transformed parameters{
> ordered[2] mu_2;
> mu_2 <- sort_asc(mu_2s);

you can jut declare mu_2 directly as an ordered[2] parameter.
That actually should help some with mixing because otherwise,
the mu_2s aren't identified (only the sorted ones are).

And to address the last other email, if you have mass around
two different local modes in the posterior, you technically
want to integrate over both for inference.

In general, mixtures are very hard, and often people just
go with a fit around a single local mode (typical in LDA
models, for example) because the entire posterior's known
to be intractable. There are some approaches, but I don't know
of any system that really solves the problem in a satisfying
way. Maybe others will have suggestions.

- Bob

I know you're not a fan of model selection, but rather model averaging for prediction, but isn't placing probabilities on models with nested parameters essentially one method of model selection?
That is, if a more complex model adds more 'noise' than predictive power due to the uncertainty in the greater number of parameters, then a simpler model could be favored.
Isn't that why bayes factors (I know you also don't like bayes factors )have a natural 'occams razor' to it? More model complexity without sufficient predictive power allows simpler models to be 'more probable' on average.

Oh, thanks!

I didn't know Stan could sample ordered vectors directly.

And for inference and prediction, yes, one should integrate over all modes.
I'm comfortable with that, since it's straightforwardly telling you there are a few probable solutions to the model.

However, knowing the "true" model, I'm trying to see how to recover the "true" model.

I know  others who use ML for mixtures do basically what you said -- Choose one probable solution/combination of the perhaps many that maximize the likelihood.

On Wednesday, February 24, 2016 at 7:31:00 PM UTC-6, Bob Carpenter wrote:
This doesn't help with mixing, but it's more efficient
computationally to use a single prior with a beta
prior than a simplex[2] with a Dirichlet prior (the
second component of the simplex is just one minus the
first).

And rather than this:

>    vector[2] mu_2s; //unsorted mu, to be sorted later
>
>     vector<lower=0>[1] sigma_1;
>     vector<lower=0>[2] sigma_2;
> }
> transformed parameters{
>     ordered[2] mu_2;
>     mu_2 <- sort_asc(mu_2s);

you can jut declare mu_2 directly as an ordered[2] parameter.
That actually should help some with mixing because otherwise,
the mu_2s aren't identified (only the sorted ones are).

And to address the last other email, if you have mass around
two different local modes in the posterior, you technically
want to integrate over both for inference.

In general, mixtures are very hard, and often people just
go with a fit around a single local mode (typical in LDA
models, for example) because the entire posterior's known
to be intractable.  There are some approaches, but I don't know
of any system that really solves the problem in a satisfying
way.  Maybe others will have suggestions.

- Bob

I just don’t see the point.  Suppose the larger model is expressed so that the smaller model corresponds to certain parameters in the larger model being set to 0.  You want to use a prior that is a mix of a point mass at 0 and some other stuff.  I’d rather just set a reasonable prior and go from there.

http://andrewgelman.com/2004/12/10/against_parsimo/

On Feb 24, 2016, at 8:43 PM, Stephen Martin <hwki...@gmail.com> wrote:

I know you're not a fan of model selection, but rather model averaging for prediction, but isn't placing probabilities on models with nested parameters essentially one method of model selection?
That is, if a more complex model adds more 'noise' than predictive power due to the uncertainty in the greater number of parameters, then a simpler model could be favored.
Isn't that why bayes factors (I know you also don't like bayes factors )have a natural 'occams razor' to it? More model complexity without sufficient predictive power allows simpler models to be 'more probable' on average.

On Wednesday, February 24, 2016 at 7:24:11 PM UTC-6, Andrew Gelman wrote:
If it can be k=1 or k=2, it will be k=2.  You can just fit the k=2 mixture model and look at your inferences.

Here is the full model:

x1 <- rnorm(100)
x2 <- rnorm(50,5,2)
x <- c(x1,x2)

mixMeta <- "
data {
    int N;
    vector[N] y;
}
transformed data {
    int Kappa;
    Kappa <- 2;
}

parameters {
    simplex[Kappa] pk; //p(K = 1), p(K=2)
    // Problem: We need several simplex arrays for each K model; can't use simplex theta[N], because all simplexes must be specified
    // For the time being, I'm doing this manually, assuming Kappa = 2
    simplex[2] theta_2[N]; //p(k_i = 1) in K=2
    simplex[2] alpha_2; //p(k = 1) in K = 2

    vector[1] mu_1; //mu in K = 1
    vector[2] mu_2s; //unsorted mu, to be sorted later

    vector<lower=0>[1] sigma_1;
    vector<lower=0>[2] sigma_2;
}
transformed parameters{
    ordered[2] mu_2;
    mu_2 <- sort_asc(mu_2s);
}
model {
    vector[2] lp;
    vector[2] lp_s;
// Priors
    // Means
    mu_1 ~ normal(0,5);
    mu_2 ~ normal(0,5);

    // SDs
    sigma_1 ~ cauchy(0,5);
    sigma_2 ~ cauchy(0,5);

    // theta weights (within K models)
    for(i in 1:N){
        theta_2[i] ~ dirichlet(alpha_2);
    }
    alpha_2 ~ dirichlet(rep_vector(1.0,2));

// Likelihoods
    for(i in 1:N){
        // K = 1
        lp[1] <- log(pk[1]) + normal_log(y[i],mu_1,sigma_1);

        // K = 2
        lp_s[1] <- log(theta_2[i,1]) + normal_log(y[i],mu_2[1],sigma_2[1]);
        lp_s[2] <- log(theta_2[i,2]) + normal_log(y[i],mu_2[2],sigma_2[2]);
        lp[2] <- log(pk[2]) + log_sum_exp(lp_s[1],lp_s[2]);

        // Increment
        increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(lp));
    }
}
"

# Label switching problem; cycles between labels
# One solution is to use an ordered vector (ordered) and use softmax to produce an ordered simplex
# Another is to constrain mu_2 to be > mu_1 through a constraint
stanOut <- stan(model_code = mixMeta,data = list(y=x,N=150),chains = 4,cores=4,iter = 10000,thin=4)

I also just realized that my likelihood was incorrect (it was weighting pk *way* too much; log(pk) should only weight the model likelihoods once, not N times).

I think by fixing it, it stabilized the chains and allowed them to converge properly.

Moreover, when the true model is not a mixture, p(k=1|D) > p(k=2|D), and when the true model is a mixture, it flips. Perfect!
It also accurately recovered the means, sds, and membership probabilities when K=2.

On Wednesday, February 24, 2016 at 7:46:37 PM UTC-6, Stephen Martin wrote:
Oh, thanks!

I didn't know Stan could sample ordered vectors directly.

And for inference and prediction, yes, one should integrate over all modes.
I'm comfortable with that, since it's straightforwardly telling you there are a few probable solutions to the model.

However, knowing the "true" model, I'm trying to see how to recover the "true" model.

I know  others who use ML for mixtures do basically what you said -- Choose one probable solution/combination of the perhaps many that maximize the likelihood.

On Wednesday, February 24, 2016 at 7:31:00 PM UTC-6, Bob Carpenter wrote:
This doesn't help with mixing, but it's more efficient
computationally to use a single prior with a beta
prior than a simplex[2] with a Dirichlet prior (the
second component of the simplex is just one minus the
first).

And rather than this:

>    vector[2] mu_2s; //unsorted mu, to be sorted later
>
>     vector<lower=0>[1] sigma_1;
>     vector<lower=0>[2] sigma_2;
> }
> transformed parameters{
>     ordered[2] mu_2;
>     mu_2 <- sort_asc(mu_2s);

you can jut declare mu_2 directly as an ordered[2] parameter.
That actually should help some with mixing because otherwise,
the mu_2s aren't identified (only the sorted ones are).

And to address the last other email, if you have mass around
two different local modes in the posterior, you technically
want to integrate over both for inference.

In general, mixtures are very hard, and often people just
go with a fit around a single local mode (typical in LDA
models, for example) because the entire posterior's known
to be intractable.  There are some approaches, but I don't know
of any system that really solves the problem in a satisfying
way.  Maybe others will have suggestions.

- Bob

x1 <- rnorm(100)
x2 <- rnorm(50,5,2)
x <- c(x1,x2)

mixMeta <- "
data {
    int N;
    vector[N] y;
}
transformed data {
    int Kappa;
    Kappa <- 2;
}

parameters {
    simplex[Kappa] pk; //p(K = 1), p(K=2)
    // Problem: We need several simplex arrays for each K model; can't use simplex theta[N], because all simplexes must be specified
    // For the time being, I'm doing this manually, assuming Kappa = 2
    simplex[2] theta_2[N]; //p(k_i = 1) in K=2
    simplex[2] alpha_2; //p(k = 1) in K = 2

    vector[1] mu_1; //mu in K = 1
    vector[2] mu_2s; //unsorted mu, to be sorted later

    vector<lower=0>[1] sigma_1;
    vector<lower=0>[2] sigma_2;
}
transformed parameters{
    ordered[2] mu_2;
    mu_2 <- sort_asc(mu_2s);
}
model {
    vector[2] lp;
    vector[2] lp_s;
// Priors
    // Means
    mu_1 ~ normal(0,5);
    mu_2 ~ normal(0,5);

    // SDs
    sigma_1 ~ cauchy(0,5);
    sigma_2 ~ cauchy(0,5);

    // theta weights (within K models)
    for(i in 1:N){
        theta_2[i] ~ dirichlet(alpha_2);
    }
    alpha_2 ~ dirichlet(rep_vector(1.0,2));

// Likelihoods
    for(i in 1:N){
        // K = 1
        lp[1] <- log(pk[1]) + normal_log(y[i],mu_1,sigma_1);

        // K = 2
        lp_s[1] <- log(theta_2[i,1]) + normal_log(y[i],mu_2[1],sigma_2[1]);
        lp_s[2] <- log(theta_2[i,2]) + normal_log(y[i],mu_2[2],sigma_2[2]);
        lp[2] <- log(pk[2]) + log_sum_exp(lp_s[1],lp_s[2]);

        // Increment
        increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(lp));
    }
}
"

# Label switching problem; cycles between labels
# One solution is to use an ordered vector (ordered) and use softmax to produce an ordered simplex
# Another is to constrain mu_2 to be > mu_1 through a constraint
stanOut <- stan(model_code = mixMeta,data = list(y=x,N=150),chains = 4,cores=4,iter = 10000,thin=4)

Generally, I am for complex models for the same reasons you express. The world is complex, and thus for the best predictive model one should model it with the complexity it warrants.

However, for 1) testing particular hypotheses 2) pitting two competing theoretical models against each other and 3) for fairly niche questions, I do indeed need to compare whether a simpler model is explanatory "enough".

Eventually, I am going to be converting a fairly complex bayesian model to Stan that assesses the probability and extent of DIF in various CFA and IRT models assuming latent groups are present.
The model requires the techniques used in the opening post, which is why I'm trying to get my feet wet in this particular example before converting the more complex model to Stan.
In that model, we do not want to marginalize over items' probabilities of exhibiting DIF to predict anything; we actually want the probability of items exhibiting DIF, because that guides our decision about the scale itself.
For that, we need to pit models against one another to make a decision.

Here is the full model:

x1 <- rnorm(100)
x2 <- rnorm(50,5,2)
x <- c(x1,x2)

mixMeta <- "
data {
    int N;
    vector[N] y;
}
transformed data {
    int Kappa;
    Kappa <- 2;
}

parameters {
    simplex[Kappa] pk; //p(K = 1), p(K=2)
    // Problem: We need several simplex arrays for each K model; can't use simplex theta[N], because all simplexes must be specified
    // For the time being, I'm doing this manually, assuming Kappa = 2
    simplex[2] theta_2[N]; //p(k_i = 1) in K=2
    simplex[2] alpha_2; //p(k = 1) in K = 2

    vector[1] mu_1; //mu in K = 1
    vector[2] mu_2s; //unsorted mu, to be sorted later

    vector<lower=0>[1] sigma_1;
    vector<lower=0>[2] sigma_2;
}
transformed parameters{
    ordered[2] mu_2;
    mu_2 <- sort_asc(mu_2s);
}
model {
    vector[2] lp;
    vector[2] lp_s;
// Priors
    // Means
    mu_1 ~ normal(0,5);
    mu_2 ~ normal(0,5);

    // SDs
    sigma_1 ~ cauchy(0,5);
    sigma_2 ~ cauchy(0,5);

    // theta weights (within K models)
    for(i in 1:N){
        theta_2[i] ~ dirichlet(alpha_2);
    }
    alpha_2 ~ dirichlet(rep_vector(1.0,2));

// Likelihoods
    for(i in 1:N){
        // K = 1
        lp[1] <- log(pk[1]) + normal_log(y[i],mu_1,sigma_1);

        // K = 2
        lp_s[1] <- log(theta_2[i,1]) + normal_log(y[i],mu_2[1],sigma_2[1]);
        lp_s[2] <- log(theta_2[i,2]) + normal_log(y[i],mu_2[2],sigma_2[2]);
        lp[2] <- log(pk[2]) + log_sum_exp(lp_s[1],lp_s[2]);

        // Increment
        increment_log_prob(log_sum_exp(lp));
    }
}
"

# Label switching problem; cycles between labels
# One solution is to use an ordered vector (ordered) and use softmax to produce an ordered simplex
# Another is to constrain mu_2 to be > mu_1 through a constraint
stanOut <- stan(model_code = mixMeta,data = list(y=x,N=150),chains = 4,cores=4,iter = 10000,thin=4)

> On Feb 24, 2016, at 8:46 PM, Stephen Martin <hwki...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Oh, thanks!
>
> I didn't know Stan could sample ordered vectors directly.
>
> And for inference and prediction, yes, one should integrate over all modes.
> I'm comfortable with that, since it's straightforwardly telling you there are a few probable solutions to the model.
>
> However, knowing the "true" model, I'm trying to see how to recover the "true" model.

That won't always work (though I'm glad to see it did here after
some debugging).

Let's say I actually know the model p(y, theta) and use it to
generate a simulated data set y' given parameters theta'.
It's still possible that the posterior p(theta | y') is
multimodal and/or to has a posterior mean other than theta'.
The only thing we can hope is that the model's calibrated and
captures the true value of theta in the 50% (or 95% or whatever)
interval 50% (95%) of the time. Of course, defining something
like a 50% interval is tricky when the model's multimodal. But
it shouldn't matter how you define it for the calibration.

- Bob

P.S. What you're doing is exactly what we always recommend---start
with a simple model and simulate data and make sure the model is
well calibrated in recovering the parameters. The reason we
recommend it is exactly as you reported---it lets you debug your
code and model pathologies. Thanks for sharing.
